lesson.title: Why Language Gets Harder to Learn as the Window Closes
lesson.summary: The critical period hypothesis holds that there is a biologically limited window, roughly ending around puberty, in which language is acquired most easily and completely, though the evidence for a hard cutoff is more mixed than often assumed.
lesson.body:
The critical period hypothesis for language proposes that there is a limited biological window, roughly from early childhood through puberty, during which the brain is especially well suited to acquiring language, and that language learned after this window tends to be acquired more slowly and less completely, particularly for grammar and native-like pronunciation. This idea extends the general concept of language acquisition by asking not just how children acquire language, but whether timing itself is part of the biological story, and it connects to adolescent development because puberty is often treated as the rough marker where the window is thought to narrow or close.

Some of the clearest supporting evidence comes from research on deaf individuals who were not exposed to any language, spoken or signed, until later in childhood because of limited access to accessible language input early on. Compared to deaf individuals exposed to sign language from infancy, those with delayed first exposure to any language tend to show weaker ultimate grammatical mastery, even after years of later practice. This kind of evidence is valuable precisely because it isolates the timing of first language exposure from other confounding factors in a way that is otherwise very hard to study ethically in humans.

The case of Genie is frequently mentioned alongside this topic, and it deserves to be handled carefully rather than treated as a clean experiment. Genie was a girl discovered in the early 1970s who had been kept in extreme isolation and abuse for most of her childhood, with essentially no language exposure. After being found, she learned some vocabulary but never developed typical grammatical competence, and researchers have often cited her case as suggestive support for a critical period. It is important to be honest about the real limits of what her case can prove. Genie's history involved severe deprivation, malnutrition, social isolation, and trauma all at once, not language deprivation alone, so it is impossible to cleanly separate the effect of missing a language window from the effects of the broader abuse she suffered. Her case also involved only one child studied under chaotic, non-experimental, and ethically fraught circumstances, including disputes among the researchers involved about how the case was handled, so it functions as a single, deeply tragic case study rather than rigorous scientific proof, and it should be presented that way rather than as a decisive experiment.

The broader scientific picture on a critical period for language is genuinely mixed rather than fully settled. There is fairly strong evidence for some sensitive period effects, especially for grammar and for accent-free pronunciation, where later learners more consistently show a foreign accent and other certain grammatical patterns even after extensive practice. But many researchers now describe this as a sensitive period rather than a strict critical period, meaning language learning becomes gradually harder and less complete with age rather than snapping shut at one fixed point, and plenty of people who begin learning a second language well after puberty still achieve very high, functional fluency, even if subtle differences from native speakers sometimes remain. The honest summary is that timing matters for language learning, but exactly how strict, how universal, and how single-cause that window is remains an active area of research rather than a fully closed question.
